docs.title: How to add all variable names to Eviews
docs.text:
How to get all the variable names in a workfile?

1) Create a group (ctrl + click on the series in the workfile and double click, then go to open as group) 2) Name the group "group_name"

3) string list_name = "" for !i = 1 to group_name.@count list_name = list_name + " " + group_name.@seriesname(!i)

How to get all exogenous variables in a workfile?

1) Open the model object (there must be a model object) 2) Go to the variable view (either View > Variable or the Variable button) 3) Click on Filter/Sort and sort FIRST by Type 4) Select all the Exogenous variables 5) right click and select 'copy' 6) select all variables in the dialog box that shows up 7) copy these into a variable in a .prg file

Alternatively, go to the model object and use the data members .@exovarlist or .@endovarlist

docs.title: How to graph multiple variables in a graph using a loop (Eviews)
docs.text:
If you have a list of variables say var_list as a string list you can do the following

for %v {var_list}
    graph name_of_var_{%v} {%v}_25a {%v}_25a_MH
next

This assumes the string list contains the prefixes for the variables and the variables with the suffixes also exist.

For example if the string list is "CDHUS and CSUS" then the above code will create the following:

  • A graph object (stored in the workfile) named "name_of_var_CDHUS"
  • A graph object (stored in the workfile) named "name_of_var_CSUS"

Each graph will contain the graphs of variables CDHUS_25a and CDHUS_25a_MH.

Note

This means CDHUS_25a an CDHUS_25a_MH must both exist in the workfile!

docs.title: Commonly used Native Eviews Functions and their Definitions
docs.text:
@count(x) returns the number of all observations (including missing values)

d(x) first difference.

d(x,n) n-th order difference.

@demean(s[,smpl]) demean. Returns a copy of series s translated to have a mean of zero.

dlog(x) first difference in logs.

dlog(x, n) nth difference in logs.

@iff(s,x,y) recode by condition returns if condition is true; otherwise returns . Note this is the same as @recode.

@obs(x[,s]) number of observations. Returns the number of non-missing observations for X in the current sample.

@pch(x)one-period percentage change (in decimal).

@pc(x) one-period percentage change (in percent) - equals @pch(x)*100.

@pca(x) one-period percentage change—annualized (in percent) equals @pcha(x)*100.

@recode(s,x,y) recode by condition. If s is true then it returns x, and s is false it returns y.

@ytd(s[, smpl]) YTD of series s. Provides the cumulative sum of a series within the year. Optionally, a sample may be provided to limit the observations included in the summation.

docs.title: Windows Command Prompt (BATCH)
docs.text:
Windows Command Prompt is a simple yet powerful language for controlling the Windiws OS.

Note

In order to get to the command prompt search cmd in the search field in Windows.

Alternatively press Win + R and type cmd and press Enter.

When the command prompt opens you will see C:\> or C:\Users> indicating your current drive is the C drive and, in the second case, that you are in the users directory (aka folder) on the C drive.

cd will change the current directory to the path that follows the cd command. For example if you are in C:\> then you can get to a folder called 'Public' in the users folder on the C drive by typing cd users/public.

..cd will go up one level in the directory tree. For example if you are in the users\public folder you would see C:\Users\Public> and if you wish to go back to the Users director you would type cd .. and the prompt would change to C:\Users>

`dir' will display the contents of the current folder.

mkdir will create a folder in the current directory. It must be followed by the name of the folder. For example C:\users> mkdir new_folder would create a new folder called new_folder in the users directory.

rmdir removes a directory. Example: rmdir new_folder would remove the folder new_folder from users.

copywill copy a file. Example: if you are in C;> you can type copy users\tap9000\file.txt users\public\backup.txt to copy a file in the tap9000 folder to the public folder (or the same folder).

del deletes a file. del filename.txt

move moves a file. move location_old\file.txt location_new\new_name_for_file.txt

Once you navigate to where a file is you can run it by calling the file name with .exe, for example myprogram.exe provided your current directory is there 'myprogram.exe' is located. You can also specify the full path to where the program is located C:\Users\Programs\myprogram.exe

cls clears the screen

exit closes the command prompt

echo prints text, for example echo Hello World!

help will list available commands

type displays the contents of a text file directly in the command prompt

Important

In order to access folders with spaces one must use quotation marks.

For example cd C:\Users> cd C:\Users\tap9000\saved games will give an error but cd "C:\Users> cd "C:\Users\tap9000\saved games" will run without an error.

docs.title: The Pipe Operator
docs.text:
The pipe operator (|) takes the output of one command and uses it as the input of another.

For example dir|more. The dir command tells the Command Prompt to show items in the current folder, more tells the CP to list them one page at a time (useful for folders containing many objects).

dir|find "report" lists files in the current folder but only shows lines that contain the word "report"

docs.title: Multiple Pipes
docs.text: type bigfile.txt | find "error" | more this will show the file contents, find files with lines with "error" and output one page at a time

docs.title: > redirects output
docs.text: dir > files.txt saves the list of tiles in the current directory to a file named 'files.txt'

docs.title: Dict Operations in Python
docs.text:
If D is a dict:

  • Retrieve values safely 

    D.get(key)
    Returns the value associated with the key without raising a KeyError.

  • View keys, values, and items 

    D.keys()
D.values()
D.items()

  • Add to a dict using .update 

    D.update({key: value})

  • Insert only if not present with .setdefault 

    D.setdefault("UR", 3.2)
    Adds the key-value pair only if the key is not already in the dict.

  • Remove and return a value with .pop 

    value = D.pop("key", None)

  • Remove and return the last key-value pair (LIFO) with .popitem 

    k, v = D.popitem()
print(k, v)

  • Empty the dict with .clear 

    D.clear()

  • Shallow copy with .copy 

    D2 = D.copy()

  • Create a new dict from keys 

    keys = ["GDP", "CPI"]
D = dict.fromkeys(keys, 0)
    Creates a new dict with the given keys and all values set to 0.

  • Merge using | (Python 3.9+) 

    d1 = {"GDP": 2.4}
d2 = {"CPI": 1.8}
merged = d1 | d2

  • Update in place using |= (Python 3.9+) 

    d1 |= {"UR": 6.1}
    Adds the new key-value pair to d1.

docs.title: Every command in Eviews falls into one of four categories:
docs.text:
• object declaration/assignment,
  • object view/procedure view,
  • interactive commands (these create unnamed objects),
  • auxiliary commands (these are commands that do not specifically pertain to objects, eg 'store').

docs.title: Command Capture:
docs.text:
when you point and click this window captures the commands being used. To activate: display command capture window by clicking on Window > Display Command Capture Window from the main EViews menu.

Figure 1.1: How to display the Command Window

To echo any commands in this window, go to Options > General Options and click on the Command settings.

Figure 1.2: Setting up the Command Window to Echo Commands

You can then save the contents by copy and paste or right clicking and saving directly. Some EVews commands are not capture enabled (because of course there are exceptions, EViews loves exceptions to their rules!).

Note

The insertion cursor can be at any place in the line of code you wish to execute, once the user hits enter that line will execute (even in the middle of a line of code).

Scroll up and down previous commands using CRTL + UP or CRTL + DOWN respectively.

The Command Explorer window (appearing on the far left of the screen) allows for a way to display context specific documentation while working in Eviews.

Once the window is opened, clicking on the name of an object type will open a documentation page for that object in a browser window.

For example, if a user wanted to know what the command @recode does they can go to the command explorer and this will take them to the Eviews website:

Note the wildcard "*" can be used for search for commands.

If a workfile is open you can use CRTL + SPACE to autocomplete commands and for objects (the manual claims this but it can be buggy).

Many commands can be linked together and saved as a program. File > New > Program will start a new program.

docs.title: Object declaration:
docs.text:
Object_type(options) object_name, below are all the possible types of object in Eviews.

The various object types :

To create an object we start the code with the object type.

For example, to create a series called lgdp we would use:

series lgdp

To create an equation called eq1 one would use:

equation eq1

docs.title: Declaring matrices and coefs:
docs.text:
matrix(m, n) x creates an empty m by n matrix named x

coef(10) results creates a 10 element coefficient vector named results

Object assignment: "=" assigns a value or values to an object.

For example:

series new_series = 0 creates a series (whose length is determined by the sample size using the smpl function) which contains zero as every entry.

Note

In order to tell Eviews which data to work on use the smpl function like so: smpl 1990q1 2025q1. Users can select the entire sample using smpl @all and can select from the beginning or to the end useing @first and @last respectively.

For example, to select from the second quarter of 2005 to the end of the data series type

smpl 2005q2 @last

When ready to work with the entire data set remember to use

smple @all

Warning

If you have the sample set (using the smpl command) to only a part of the data set then any commands given will apply only to that sample of the dataset! Always use smpl @all when finished altering a subsample of the dataset.

docs.title: Object Commands
docs.text:
These can be used to modify existing objects, for example eq1.ls log(cons) c x1 x2 this estimates an equation by OLS (LS for 'least squares")

To add to systems or groups use the following (similar to methods in Python OOP)

sys1.append y = c(1) c(2)*x this adds the equation to the system called sys1 group01.add gdp cons inc g x this adds the variables to the left of .add to the group named goup01

We can change the values in a series in a single command by specifying the sample period smpl @first 1979 eries dummy = 1 this will make all values from the first obs to the obs at 1979 to equal 1

docs.title: Commands:
docs.text:
show displays, do executes procedures, if the object window is already open then show is the same as do, freeze creates a table or graph of the object view and print prints the object view window.

Note

The show action is assumed for view commands and do is assumed for procedures.

For example gdp.line is the same as show gpd.line (which creates a line graph of the variable named gdp)

Another example:

eq1.ls cons c gdp is the same as do eq1.ls cons gdp

The print command can be used to print and the print(l)

docs.title: Freeze:
docs.text: freeze gdp.linecreates and untitled graph or table from a view specification, but freeze(figure1) gdp.bar creates a bar graph named figure 1.

docs.title: Some examples of object commands that can be used on series:
docs.text:
Sheet, hist, freq,bar, correl, lrvar, uroot, stats, label(r) shows a spreadsheet, histogram, bar graph, correlation, unit root test, or labels the series respectively.

Every object has native Data Members which can be retrieved using the following after "." and the variable name

Groups also have @count which returns the number of objects in the group.

Equations have members like @r (r -squared) or @f(f-statistic).

docs.title: Interactive commands: these create new unnamed objects:
docs.text:
For example:

ls y c x1 x2 will run OLS y = c + beta_1x1 + beta_2x2 and create an untitled equation object to hold the results

Example 2:

scatt x y creates a group and a scatterplot (unnamed).

Warning

Unnamed object scannot be referenced by name, saved to disk or deleted EXCEPT though the graphical Windows interface! Using named objects is typically preferred if using code to control Eviews.

In contrast to the above we can do the following

equation eq1.ls y cy x1 x2 and now the equation is named eq1

We can also do:

group mygroup x y now the group is named mygroup

mygroup.scat

docs.title: Aux commands:
docs.text: Aux commands are commands such as "store" (to save a file) that do not pertain to a particular object . Syntax: command(option_list) argument_list

docs.title: Workfiles and Databases
docs.text:
wfcreate this creates a new workfile (followed by the name of the new workfile and an option for frequency of the data)

For example:

wfcreate macro1 u 1 1000 creates a workfile called macro1 which is undated/unstructured and contains 1000 obs

while

wfcreate macro1 q 1965q1 2025q4 creates a quarterly workfile from the first quarter of 1965 to the last quarter of 2025.

The letters "wf" precede workfile commands, thus in order to open a workfile we use wfopen, to save use wfsave (eg: wfsave a:\my_work_file).

Note

To close a workfile we use close my_work_file (not wfclose as one might guess)

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Databases are referred to as 'db' so dpcreate creates a database while dbopenopens a database etc (TODO: Add database commands)

Note

db ttself is a command. db C:\evdata\usdb opens a data base called usdb if it already exists and creates one if it does not exist.

Other useful commands: dbrename, dbdelete, dbcopy

docs.title: Copying:
docs.text:
copy source_name destination_name

Note

The source_name and destination_name can contain a full workfile address starting with a page name and then a variable name. EG copy page1/var1 page2/var2 would copy var1 on page1 to var2 on page2.

Note

Eveiws supports wildcards: * for multiple characters and ? for single characters. The patterns must match (see below).

rename source_name destination_name

delete name_pattern deletes the objects with this PATTERN (can use wildcards here)

docs.title: What is a model in EViews?
docs.text:
A model is a set of equations that jointly describe the relationship between a set of variables (vars). These equations are combined into a single Model object in Eviews 12. Models allow for the simulation of different assumptions about variables that are determined outside the model (I.E. exogenous variables or "exovars").

A model in its most general form is F(y,x) = 0 where F is a vector of (real valued) functions, y is the endogenous variables and x is the exogenous variables. F is defined as LHS (Endogenous variables) minus RHS (usually a linear combination of Exogenous variables) and therefore F = 0 means RHS = LHS for the system.

Each equation (eqn) must have a unique endogenous variable (endovar) attached to it (on the LHS).

In Equation (49.2) from the textbook 

- y_i is the unique endogenous variable,
- f_i(y, x) is the function for that endogenous variable and this function depends on any or all other y and any or all other x in the system.

Note

For example, if GDP at time t is y_i then on the RHS we could have GDP_(t-1) as a y argument in f_i.

docs.title: Equations:
docs.text:
Equations can be inline or linked.

Inline equations are written in as text, whereas linked equations bring specification from an external EV object (e.g. an estimation object or even another Model object).

Equations can be stochastic or identities.

Identities hold exactly, stochastic relationships hold with a random error.

docs.title: SOLVING THE MODEL
docs.text:
If you solve a given model then: given exogenous variables X, EVeiws 12 finds values Y that satisfy the system.

Note

Solving does NOT mean finding coefficients that minimize a loss function, rather solving means finding values of the endovars that satisfy the entire system, the coefs are fixed, either user specified or solved previously.

When solving a Model, Eviews must first associate data with each variable in the model: Eviews binds each of the model variables to a series in the workfile (

Note

the software creates aliases when binding, e.g. Y becomes Y_0.

Eviews then solves the model for each observation in the selected sample and places the results in the corresponding series.

docs.title: Aliasing:
docs.text:
When a model is solved, aliasing is usually applied to the endogenous variables so that historical data is not overwritten. For models which contain lagged endogenous variables, aliasing allows users to bind the lagged variables to either of the following:

  • (1) the actual historical data (this is called a static forecast)
  • (2) the values solved for in previous periods (this is called a dynamic forecast).

Either way the lagged endovars are treated as exovars when solving the model for a single period.

Aliasing is also applied to exovars when doing scenarios (S). Creating a S means making changes to exovars or Add Factors.

!!! note Add Factors (AFs) are manual changes made to the residuals of a system eqn or change made directly to the endovars. In either case the results is directly altering the output of the model. That is to say, AFs change the forecast endovar vals after solving a model.

docs.title: How do Scenarios work?
docs.text:
In a S users can change the path of an EXOGENOUS variable by OVERRIDING the variable. (Contrast this with the role of an AF which is to change the Endovars – IE the model's output directly).

When an exovar is overridden under a given S, the variable is copied and given a suffix (e.g. _25A) – this is called binding.

docs.title: For example: If we have a historical endovar called Y, a given historical exovar might be called X.  In that case when we run the model to create a forecast (called a baseline forecast because we have not altered any exovars – in our example, we have not altered X) Eviews will create a forecast and bind the newly created forecast to a variable with a "_0" suffix, in this case Y_0.
docs.text:
If we then create a Scenario (by default called Scenario_1) then we can alter or "override" X and run a new forecast using an the newly altered/overridden X. The altered exovar X will be bound to a new series and given a suffix (Eg in this case it might be called X_1) and the new forecast values (and historical values) for Y under Scenario_1 will also be bound to a new variable and given a suffix (by default the suffix is "_1" making the new variable Y_1.)

note !!! Summary: under a baseline scenario we have one set of (usually accurate historical) values for exovars X which lead to a baseline forecast for Y. During the process of forecasting Eviews creates a new series for Y adds the suffix "_0" to create Y_0. If we then create a Scenario (by default called Scenario_1) by overriding X this means we are altering historical X and this altered version is bound to a variable with a suffix ("_1" by default) say X_1). This change in X (the altered series is called X_1) leads to new forecasts for Y, which Eviews will label Y_1( by default).

note !!! Users can create user defined suffixes for scenarios in Eviews, at TDE we use suffixes that indicate the scenario (by letter) and the year, eg "_25A" for scenario A in 2025.

docs.title: ADD FACTORS (AFs)
docs.text:
AFs are a special kind of exovar used to shift the output of an equation. This means the AFs change the output of the model directly.

In contrast to AFs, under a given S say Scenario_1, we use a modified version of our exovar X (called X_1) to solve the model and this therefore changes the output of the model.

Using an Add Factor under any given scenario changes the values in Y directly (either by adding the AF to the residual of the equation or adding the AF to the endovar directly). Rather than creating a copy of the endovar series Eviews binds the AF to a new variable with _A as a suffix.

Thus if we have Y as historical data, Y_1 as Y under Scenario 1 with X_1 as X under Scenario 1 and we then use an AF we will have Y_A as a separate series that tells is how Y_1 was altered.

docs.title: Modelling
docs.text:
*EXAMPLE MODEL (TODO: make clearer and add pictures of steps taken) Having set up a model we can solve it as Deterministic for simulation type (deterministic means there is no simulation of errors and therefore no SD bands included in the simulation) and under Dynamics we can select Static. Dynamics = Static means we are looking at one step ahead forecasts over the existing data.

Under "Solution Sample" set the sample over which to solve the model to avoid using missing values. Once solved the results for the ENDOVARS are placed into a series in the workfile their names are determined by the aliasing given by the user.

PICTURE OF THE WINDOW IN WHICH DETERMINISTIC IS CHOSEN HERE In Variable View each variable is given a type (En for endo. X for Exo, and A for add factor (double check this). If the variable is black it is an EXOVAR, if it is blue it is being "traced" ( "traced" means that the intermediate values of the variable obtained during solving the model are stored, usually used for diagnosing why a model does not converge) and if a variable in the variable view is red it is being overridden this means there is an altered version of the exovar that is being used. PICTURE OF THE VARIABLE VIEW WITH VARIOUS TYPES OF VARIABLES HERE

Why have a variable view? For endovar Y we may have actual Y called Y, baseline forecast Y called Y_0, scenario 1 (or scenario A) forecast values of Y called Y1.

We can make graphs for actual and fitted values as follows: select variables (ctrl + click) and use proc > make graph. Be sure to set the correct sample in Sample For Graph.

Example of static solution, one step ahead forecast:

Performing a Dynamic Solution:

We use this to forecast past actual historical data and therefore use our own forecasted values as the basis for subsequent forecasts. To reiterate, here we are doing forecasts at multiple horizons and using forecast values as the basis for the multi step forecast. To do this click "solve" in the Model window (i.e. open the model by double clicking it) and then choose "Dynamic solution" in the Dynamics section of the dialog. If our data goes up to 1999 and we select 1985 1999 in the solution sample then the model forecasts using HISTORICAL EXOVARS but FORECASTED ENDOVARS for those periods. To reiterate, if we do dynamic forecasts over a period where we have actual exovar data then the system uses forecast endovar vals but actual exovar data, this is therefore counterfactual with respect to the exovars since in a real forecast we would have perfect insight into the future values of the exovars of the future.

This means our forecast shows how well the model would have worked under a very specific set of assumptions: (1) we use our model to forecast future endovar values, (2) we use our forecast endovar values to compute future forecasts (3) we have perfect knowledge of the future values of the EXOVARS until the end of our sample.

USING THE MODEL TO FORECAST FUTURE VALUES OF THE ENDOVARS (into the future for which we do not have exovar data)

Chose values for the exovars, these are not forecast, they MUST be chosen by the user. Use these forecast values of the exovars to update our forecasts of the endovars.

For example, we might forecast G using an ar regression on log(g).

A Note on AFs: AFs do NOT set the values of the exovars, rather these directly change the forecast values (by changing the residuals in the modelling eqn or the values of the Endovars directly).

Using Scenarios for Alternate Assumptions:

How to see what the model will output (i.e. what values the forecast endovars will take on) with different assumed future exogenous variables? We don’t want to edit the historical data or change the variables back and forth so we can use Scenarios (S). These keep track of the different paths we assumed for exovars without writing over the data.

In a S you can choose to change a subset of the exogenous variables while leaving the rest unchanged (and can choose to alter only a subset of any given exovar also). This is to say you can change as much or as little of the exovars as you wish when creatin a S.

When the S is solved the values of the ENDOVARS are saved in the workfile with a given suffix ( the suffix "_1" is the default but this can be changed by the user, we use for example _25A for scenario A in 2025).

Two special scenarios always exist by default: Actuals and Baseline. Neither of these can have overridden variables (meaning the EXOVARS cannot be changed, not sure about add factors here). Using the Actuals writes to the original historical data vars (careful not to overwrite existing data!), Running a Baseline S appends _0 to the vars (ie Baseline works with copies of the original data).

Create a Scenario: (see page 1032 of the PDF). Override some exovars by listing them in 'override' with spaces between each. These will now appear as red in the variable view of the Model . Users can give them another suffix besides the default "_1" under aliasing tab of the scenarios dialog.

In our Baseline forecast we had to make assumptions about the values of fexovars (Future realizations of Exogenous Variables).

In Scenario 1 we simply make different assumptions about fexovar values and write these new assumed fexovar values into X_1 (where X is the historical actual exovars, X_0 is the historical exovar values plus the baseline assumed fexovar values and X_1 is the fexovar vals under Scenario 1).

Make sure to check "solve for alternative along with Active" when solving. Make sure also that the Scenario 1 (or whichever S the user is interested in) is active and Baseline is selected the alternative. Also be sure to select the solution sample eg 2000 2005.

Look at the results: proc> make graph. Set model variables to Endogenous variables. Set Solution series to Deterministic solutions and check both Active and Compare solutions check boxes. Active S1, Alternative BL. (Scenario 1 and Baseline respectively).*

docs.title: BUILDING A MODEL
docs.text:
Method 1: Create using Object > New Object and choose Model

Method 2: select a set of estimation objects (eqns, VARs, system_ and right-click and choose Open as Model.

Add equations by either selecting insert if by inputting the equation by text or drag and drop from the work file window into the model.

Linking Equations to model objects:

Use proc>Link to play with linking and unlinking (see PDF page 1036 for details)

Working with Model Structure (PDF page 1036)

There are two primary Model views: Equation View and Variable View

Eqn View: each line shows a linked object or inline (text) eqn. If there is an issue it will show up here as an error with a red line over the eqn. Examine eqns using right-click on the eqn and selecting Properties (PDF page 1037 of user guide 2 for Eviews 12). You can also use ctrl F to bring up the Model Find dialog where you may search for eqns by name. Variable View is used for adjusting options for variables and for displaying and editing series associated with the model NOTE: The only way to add a variable or to change the type of a variable in the model is to modify the model equations. In the variable window you can also see dependencies between variables by clicking Dependencies. There is also TEXT VIEW: this shows the entire structure of the model. The lines contain the eqns of the model. A line beginning with a : represents a link to an external object. A line beginning with @ADD specifies an add factor.

The add factor command is of the form @add(v) endo_var add_factor.

Note

The option (v) is used to specify that the add factor should be applied DIRECTLY to the endovar . By default, the add factor is added to the residual of the equation.

(See book page 1028, PDF page 1049 for the section on Add Factors)

A line beginning with @INNOV denotes an innovation variance which can be applied to the enovar using @innov endovar number where "number" is the Standard Deviation of the innovation applied during stochastic simulation. See PDF page 1040 of Guide 2.

Dependency Graph View( PDF page 1043).

Specifying Scenarios (PDF page 1045):

The most important function of a S (scenario) is to specify which series will be used to hold the data associated with a particular solution of the model. Aliasing allows the user to specify the alias appended to the series name (eg _25A for S_A in 2025) . S are specified by declaring which EXO variables are to be override (IE altered from their historical values). Overridden variables will draw their data from the series with the alias attached (eg "_1" or" _25A") and other exovars will draw from the series with the same name as the variable (IE variables that are not overridden contain historical data). overridden variables are the exovars being used to generate a different S. Using a S one can exclude ENDO variables as well. When an endovar equation is dropped, the value of the variable is taken directly the workfile series with the same name. This basically makes the ENDOVAR into an EXOVAR for the purposes of modelling.

docs.title: Scenario Editing tools (PDF page 1047)
docs.text:
Edit override right button menu item available from the variable view of a model lets a user exclude, override and edit ENDO and EXO vars for the current S.

In a Model object using the View button shows all S and the exclusions and overrides therein.

docs.title: Using Add Factors (PDF page 1049, book page 1028)
docs.text:
An Add Factor (AF) is an extra EXO variable that directly affects ENDO results. The most common use for AFs is to provide a smoother transition from historical data into the forecast period. Typically, add factors will be used to compensate for a poor fit of one or more equations of the model near the end of the historical data, when we suspect this will persist into the forecast period. Add factors provide an ad hoc way of trying to adjust the results of the model without respecifying or reestimating the equations of the model.

The third form is f(y_i – a) = f_i(y, x) which means altering y inside of a function in stead of altering the residual as in 49.4.

Note

If we use @add then we are adding to the residual (RHS) but if we use @add(v) we are adding the LHS of the eqn. This is only important if the LHS contains a transformation of the variable e.g. log(g), then @add(v) adds to g and the output is log(g) so the new output is log(g - a) where as the command @add adds directly to log(g) ( so the new output is log(g) = f_i(y, x) + a.

docs.title: The Easier (local) method of creating AFs:
docs.text:
Go to the equation view of the model and double click the equation of interest. Eqn Properties > go to Add Factors tab. In the Factor type box select whether you want to shift the residual (y_i = f_i(y, x) + a ) or shift the ENDOVAR (eg log(g -a) = f_i(y, x)). Click Yes to create the series that holds the add factor. It will be filled with NAs. Initialize the Add Factor:

Still in the Eqn Properties box click the Initialize Active Add Factor Button.

Zero: will set all the values of the AF (Add Factor) to zero. So that this equation has no residuals at actuals: this sets the values of the add factor, so the equation is exactly satisfied without error when the variables of the model = values in the actual series.

So that this equation has no residuals at actives: this sets the vals of the AF such that the equation is exactly satisfied when the model vars = values I in the ENDO and EXO vars associated with the active S.

So model solves the target variables to values of the trajectory series: this sets the vals of the AF such that an ENDOVAR of the model follows a particular target path then the model is solved.

Set the sample over which the AF should initialized by modifying the Initialization sample box. NOTE: if an AF is present for a given S, then it will be present for every S, but can be overridden for a particular S just like an exovar. (QUESTION: this means you cannot run the Baseline if the AF for any S is missing?)

docs.title: The Harder (global) method of creating AFs:  Initialize or override Afs for ALL equations in the model at the same time. Proc > Add Factors does this. EG to create a complete set of Afs that make the model solve to actual values over history use Add Factors > Equation Assignment… to create AF for every equation, then use Add Factors  > Set Values… to set the Afs so that all the equations have no residuals at the actual values.
Locking the Model:
docs.text: This disables changes to the model. Proc > Protect/Unprotect model. When you first lock the model you will have to put in a password with min 4 characters. Putting a pw locks down backward compatibility and also shuts down some functionality (see PDF page 1051).

docs.title: Solving the Model
docs.text:
When solving the model a number of steps are taken The Block Structure of the model is analyzed (see PDF page 1039). Variables are bound to series in the workfile, according to the override settings and name aliasing rules of the S. If an endovar is being tracked then a new series will be created, if not a temp series will created (QUESTION: what do you mean "tracked"?) EQNs of the model are solved for each obs in the solution sample using iterative algos to compute the values of the endovars. Temp series are deleted. Results are rounded. See PDF page 1052 for Stochastic simulation and for leads and lags for endovars.

See PDF page 1055 for Initialization Methods (back casting for models with MA)

Basic Options (For solving)

To solve click Solve.

This is the most important part to set for application.

docs.title: Simulation type:
docs.text:
Deterministic means all equations in the model are solved so that they hold without error during the sim period, all coefs are held fixed at their point estimates and all exovars are held constant. Result = single path for endovars which can be evaluated by solving the model once. Stochastic means all the equations are solved so they have residuals which match randomly draw errors and (optionally) the coefs and exovars are also varied randomly. The model generates a distribution of outcomes.

Note

solve the model deterministically at first to be sure it is behaving as expected and then solve stochastically.

docs.title: Dynamics box:
docs.text:
Determines how Eviews uses historical data for enovars when solving the model. If Dynamic solution is chosen then only vals of the endovars from BEFORE the solution sample are used when forming the forecast. This means lagged endovars and ARMA terms are calculated using calculated solutions from previous periods NOT THE ACTUAL HISTORICAL VALS!. A dynamic solution is typically correct to use when forecasting values several periods into the future.

Static solution means values of the endovar up to the previous period are used each time the model is solved. Lagged endovars and ARMA terms are base don actual values of the endovars. A static solution is correct when producing a set of one-step ahead forecasts over the historical data to examine historical fit. A static solution cannot be used to predict more than one obs into the future!

Fit means endovars for the current period are used when the model is solved. All endovars except the one var for the equation being evaluated are replaced with their actual values. Fit is used to examine the fit of EACH of the equations in in the model when considered separately, IGNORING THEIR INTERDEPENDENCE IN THE MODEL.

The fit option can only be used for periods when historical values are available for all the endogenous variables.

Structural checkbox: can ignore any ARMA specifications that appear in the model equations.

At bottom LEFT of the dialog is a box for the solution sample. The SS is the set of obs over which the model will be solved. Unlike in some other EViews procedures, the solution sample will not be contracted automatically to exclude missing data and the model wont run without data available for all exovars over the SS.

RHS of the dialog are controls for selecting which scenarios we would like to solve. Select Edit Scenario Options buttons users can examing settings of an S. The Solve for Alternative along with Active should be used in a STOCHASTIC SETTING where the two S must be solved together. See PDF page 1059 for stochastic options.

Tracked variables: PDF page 1063

The Tracked Variables page of the dialog lets users change which endovars are being tracked by the model. If a variable is being tracked, it means the results for that variable are saved in a series in the workfile after the simulation is complete. If a variable is not tracked, then nothing is saved from the simulation for that variable. Used for models with large numbers of variables.

Note

all variables are tracked by default.

The traced variables list allows user to specify a list of vars for which intermediate vals wil be stored during iterations of the solutions process. Look at the Trace Output view after the model is complete to see where errors may be coming from if the model is failing to converge.

docs.title: Boundaries:
docs.text:
tells the solver to give warnings if any variables cross user specified boundaries. Can be examined in the Check Solution Bounds view once solve is complete. See PDF 1064 for Solver info (algo for solving the model). Working with Model Data see PDF page 1072

Types of series available in the model window: actuals, active, alternate.

Actuals are historical data for endovars and historical data and baseline forecast for exovars. Active: the workfile series use when solving the active S. for endovars this is the series with a name plus _alias (eg _25A). For exovars it will be the actual series unless overridden. If overridden the exovars will ALSO be series with the alias appended.

Alternate: the workfile series that is used when solving the alternate scenario. The rules are the same as for active.

Editing and Displaying Data 1073 TODO

Managing Data 1075 TODO Comparing solution data 1076 The Compare solutions menu item, (from the View menu) allows users to view any difference between solution values for different S.

After solving for different S users can click on View > Compare solutions… to being up a dialog that allows for comparison of solutions across different S.

Choose which vars to compare using the Select drop-down box and the From edit field. Once a var is selected users can select S to compare using the Series to compare area. The first choice using Solution series drop-down chooses between comparing point estimates of deterministic solutions of means of stochastic solutions.

The Compare the Active Scenario drop-down allows users to choose vars for comparison.

NOTE: changing the S here will change the active S for the model and for the comparison.

Users have two choices for specifying the SECOND set of variables. Select a S using the Scenario radio button and then selecting a S OR by selecting Pattern

Pattern will match using the wildcard "" to represent variable names in the pattern. EG if the current series is I_0 then "_OLD" would specify I_OLD.

Users can ref a data based using dbname:: syntax.

The table lists any variables for which the percentage difference between the two series for each scenario is greater than the specified tolerance. The columns in the table show details about the variables.

The first shows the variable name. The second, Delta, shows the maximum difference between the two series for each variable. The third and fourth columns, “First” and “Last”, give the date (or observation number) of the first period in which the two series differ and the last period in which the two series differ. Here, the first period in which M_0 differs from M_1 is 1960Q1, and the last period in which they differ is 1999Q4.

docs.title: Programming
docs.text:
CHAPTER 6: EViews Programming

Create a new program

program program_name Generally each line corresponds to a command so each can be executed pressing enter. One can also execute selected batches by pressing crtl+Enter.

To see line numbers press wrap +/- and select Display line numbers.

Manually break long lines using the _ character:

This will execute as a single line of code (but _ must be the very LAST character on the line for this to work)

Comments are formed using the apostrophe before the text. If you wish to commend out (or uncomment) a code block right-mouse click and select Comment Selection or Uncomment Selection respectively.

Auto format by selecting right-mouse click and select Format Selection.

The Snapshot button creates a manual snapshot of the code (in case things go wrong).

Open a program:

open program_name.prg

OR

open "full file path"

Hit the run button to execute the entire program (each line in order of appearance) or use the run command. EG

run program_name

OR

run full_path_name arg1 arg2 arg 3 (see PDF page 132)

To run verbose and specify the max number of errors use

run(v, 500) program_name

To do so quietly use

run(q, 500) program_name

Note we can run programs and chose which variables to use at run time. See book page 124, PDF page 133.

run program_name(op1, opt2, opt3=k) arg0 arg1 arg1 (%0 %1 and %2 respectively).

Program Variables: two types Control variables (numeric) String variables Control variables are written with a bang at the front (! = bang)

EG

!x !1 !i !counter

These are assigned using the = sign and are not stored as variables.

NOTE: control variables are used in programs via text substitution. If EViews encounters a control variable in a program it substitutes the text value of that variable into the program. One of the implications of the text substitution is that you may lose some numeric accuracy when using a program variable due to the conversion in to and out of a text representation of the number.

String program variables are text rather than numeric and are stored for temporraty use using the % character

%value = "value in millions of US dollars"

Used to help build up command text, variable names, or other string values. An assigned string variable may appear in any expression in place of the underlying string.

docs.title: Spools
docs.text:
Chapter 4 Spools:

Spools combine output data: tables, graphs, text, other spools…this allows us to organize Eviews results as a log of output or for a presentation. See Ch 18 of Users Guide 1 book page 877.

Create a spool >> spool my_spool

A new spool can be created by printing to a nonexistent spool!

output (s) my_spool this tells EViews to send all subsequent print jobs to my_spool (see output book page 444 of command manual)

After the above command we can do the following:

tabl1.print eq1.output(p) output off

Tab1 and eq1 will both be appended to my_spool

Adding to a spool:

output (s) my_old_spool ser01.line(p) print a line graph of series 1, this is printed because of the (p) command grp01.scat(p) eq1.wald(p) c(1)=c(2)

docs.title: Ev strings
docs.text:
Chapter 5: Strings Use double quotes for a "string" in Eviews. The null string is represented as "". The null string can also be represented as a missing value.

String Operators:

(1) concatenation—plus (“+”) (2) relational—equal to (“=”), not equal to (“<>”), greater than (“>”), greater than or equal to (“>=”), less than (“<=”).

When concatenating strings the empty string is ignored (interpreted as a blank string) which means adding "" to a string will not change the string.

String Ordering: alphabetical ordering places hyphens and aposrophes before alphanumeric symbols. In terms of upper and lower case letters "a" precedes "A".

With strings greater than or less than indicates ordering, note that if the relation is true then the comparison returns a 1 and 0 otherwise:

To obtain sections or portions of a string use @left @right and @mid:

@upper and @lower turn the string into all upper or lowercase. @ltrim @rtrim and @trim ignore leading spaces (these functions do not trim the string!) The following all return 1:

Relational operators treat emptry strings as missing values so comparisons with non-empty strings produce NAs.

String Lists: a string with three words would be thought of as having 3 elements. Double quotes are used to denote multi word elements in a string list, which is to say an element in double quotes can have multiple words.

" ""this thing"" ""has exactly"" ""three elements"" " a " begins and ends the string but each multi word element is enclosed in "" also.

String Functions @length(str) the number of CHARACTERS in a string @wcount(str) integer value of the number of string elements in a string list. @wfind("I did it", "did") returns the value 2, because did is the second element in the string list

@wfindnc(str) same as above but not case sensitive

@isempty(str) 1 if empty, 0 otherwise @eqna(str1, str2) 1 if strings are equal, 0 otherwise: treats null strings as ordinary blank strings and NOT as missing values!

@neqna(str1, str2) returns 1 if strings are NOT equal and 0 otherwise. @val(str[, fmt]) converts the sting into a numeric value if possible and returns NA otherwise.

@dateval(str[,fmt]) converts a string to a date number (also see @dtoo)

String manipulation:

@left(str, int) returns a string containing the int CHARACTERS at the left of the string

@wleft(str_list, int) returns a string containing the int ELEMENTS of a string LIST to the left of the string list. @right and @wright are similar. @mid and @wmid work the same way but require can take int1 and int2 arguments (if int2 is not specified it returns the rest of the characters in the string. @mid(str, int1, int2) and @wmid(str_list, int1, int2)

@word(str_list, int) returns the int element of the string list (@wordq is the same but preserves quotes)

@wkeep(str_list, "pattern_list") returns the list of elements in str_list that match the pattern in pattern list.

EG:

@wdrop(str_list, "pattern_list") returns a string list without the elements that match the pattern list

@replace and @wreplace replace work on string list elements and patterns respectively

@replace(str1, str2, str3) within str1, find str2 and exchange it for str3 . @wreplace(str_list, “src_pattern”, “replace_pattern”)

EG: @wreplace("ABC AB", "B", "X") replaces all instances of “B” with “X”, returning the string “AXC AX”

@wintersect(str_list1, str_list2) acts like intersection of sets, same for @wunion

@wunique(str_list) removes duplicates and returns the list

@wnotin(str_list1, str_list2) returns all elements of str_list1 that are NOT in str_list2

@wsort(str_list[, "D"]) sorts elements of a list, use D for sorting in descending order

Using strings in Eviews

If making a temporarty string use the % character EG

%value = "a string of values" this will exist only during the time Eviews is running!

If you want the string to exist in general use

string string_name = "a string of values"

Viewing strings: strings can be views as a string (a list of characters) or a word list (a list of elements).

String vectors say PDF page 102.

Dates see PDF page 103

import numpy as np

import pandas as pd

See https://www.eviews.com/download/whitepapers/py2eviews.pdf for details

Note

The example in the pdf linked above says to use A for annual and Q for quarterly but the newest version of Python asks for AE and QE respectively.

import py2eviews as evp

eviewsapp = evp.GetEViewsApp(instance='new', showwindow=True)

Then call the PutPythonAsWF function to push both benchmark & indicator to EViews (into a single new workfile, but with two different pages):

evp.PutPythonAsWF(benchmark, app=eviewsapp)

evp.PutPythonAsWF(indicator, app=eviewsapp, newwf=False)

Note

Behind the scenes, PutPythonAsWF will detect the DatetimeIndex of your pandas object (if you have one) and adjust it to match EViews' date requirements. Since EViews assigns dates to be the beginning of a given period depending on the frequency, this can lead to misalignment issues and unexpected results when calculations are performed. For example, a DatetimeIndex with an annual 'YE' frequency and a date of 2000-12-31 will be assigned an internal EViews date of 2000-12-01. In this case, the PutPythonAsWF method will adjust the date to 2000-01-01 before pushing it to EViews.

Running EViews commands:

EViews commands can also be run using the Run method.

We’ll use it here to rename the two page names:

evp.Run('pageselect Untitled', app=eviewsapp)

evp.Run('pagerename Untitled annual', app=eviewsapp)

evp.Run('pageselect Untitled1', app=eviewsapp)

evp.Run('pagerename Untitled1 quarterly', app=eviewsapp)

evp.Run('copy(rho=.7, c=chowlins, overwrite) annual\\benchmark quarterly\\benchmarked @indicator indicator', app=eviewsapp)

docs.text:
<pre><code>from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Iterable, Optional, Sequence

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Optional: only import if available; keep module import cheap
try:  # pragma: no cover - environment specific
    import py2eviews as evp
except Exception:  # pragma: no cover - optional dependency
    evp = None  # type: ignore

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# String / parsing helpers
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rmv_percent(df: pd.DataFrame, cols: Sequence[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Remove percent-signs from specified columns and convert to float.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : DataFrame
        Input frame that contains percentage-like text columns.
    cols : sequence of str
        Column names to clean.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        A copy of ``df[cols]`` with ``"%"`` removed (via regex) and dtype float.

    Notes
    -----
    - Also trims whitespace and thousands separators (",") if present.
    - Non-convertible values become ``NaN``.
    """
    out = (
        df.loc[:, cols]
        .replace({"%": "", ",": ""}, regex=True)
        .apply(lambda s: pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce"))
    )
    return out


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Convenience inspection
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check(df: pd.DataFrame, start: Optional[str] = "2024Q1", end: Optional[str] = "2026Q2") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Quickly slice a PeriodIndex-ed frame to inspect a join window.

    Useful for visual checks where the historical portion is in levels and the
    forecast portion is in YoY percent change.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : DataFrame
        Quarterly PeriodIndex-ed frame.
    start, end : str or None
        Inclusive slice bounds like ``"2025Q1"``. Use ``None`` to omit a bound.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        Sliced view.
    """
    if start and end:
        return df.loc[start:end]
    if start and not end:
        return df.loc[start:]
    if end and not start:
        return df.loc[:end]
    return df


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# EViews interop
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def get_page(
    pagename: str,
    filter_: str = "*",
    instance: str = "existing",
    show: bool | str = False,
    quarterly_period: bool = True,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Pull a page from the currently open EViews workfile.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pagename : str
        EViews page name to pull.
    filter_ : str, default "*"
        Wildcard filter for variable names.
    instance : {"existing", "new"}
        See ``py2eviews.GetEViewsApp``.
    show : bool | str, default False
        Show the EViews GUI window. Accepts truthy strings for backward
        compatibility with older code.
    quarterly_period : bool, default True
        If True, convert the DatetimeIndex to a quarterly PeriodIndex.
    verbose : bool, default False
        If True, print a tail preview.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        Data fetched from EViews, optionally reindexed to ``PeriodIndex(freq='Q')``.
    """
    if evp is None:  # pragma: no cover
        raise ImportError("py2eviews is not installed/available in this environment.")

    app = evp.GetEViewsApp(instance=instance, showwindow=bool(show))
    df = evp.GetWFAsPython(app=app, pagename=pagename, namefilter=filter_)
    if quarterly_period:
        df.index = pd.PeriodIndex(df.index, freq="Q")
    if verbose:
        print(df.tail())
    return df


def select_page(page_name: str, instance: str = "existing", show: bool | str = False) -> None:
    """Select an EViews page in the current workfile.

    Parameters
    ----------
    page_name : str
        Page to select.
    instance, show : see :func:`get_page`.
    """
    if evp is None:  # pragma: no cover
        raise ImportError("py2eviews is not installed/available in this environment.")

    app = evp.GetEViewsApp(instance=instance, showwindow=bool(show))
    cmd = f"pageselect {page_name}"
    evp.Run(cmd, app=app)


def push(df: pd.DataFrame, instance: str = "existing", show: bool | str = False, newwf: bool = False) -> None:
    """Push a DataFrame to the current EViews workfile page.

    Index handling
    --------------
    - If the frame is indexed by quarterly Periods, convert to their start-of-
      quarter timestamps (EViews-friendly) before pushing.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : DataFrame
        Data to push.
    instance, show : see :func:`get_page`.
    newwf : bool, default False
        If True, create a new workfile; otherwise push to current page.
    """
    if evp is None:  # pragma: no cover
        raise ImportError("py2eviews is not installed/available in this environment.")

    app = evp.GetEViewsApp(instance=instance, showwindow=bool(show))
    out = df.copy()
    if isinstance(out.index, pd.PeriodIndex) and out.index.freqstr.upper().startswith("Q"):
        out.index = out.index.to_timestamp(how="start")
    evp.PutPythonAsWF(out, app=app, newwf=newwf)


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pandas utilities
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def get_index(df: pd.DataFrame, date: str | pd.Period) -> int:
    """Return the integer location of ``date`` in the index.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : DataFrame
    date : str or Period
        A label present in ``df.index`` (e.g., ``"2025Q4"``).
    """
    return int(df.index.get_loc(pd.Period(date, freq="Q") if isinstance(date, str) else date))


def rename_rbind(
    df1: pd.DataFrame,
    df2: pd.DataFrame,
    first_forecast_date: str,
    dropna: bool = False,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Row-bind two frames across a forecast join, aligning column names.

    ``df1`` is treated as the historical/TD baseline; ``df2`` contains a
    forecast that starts at ``first_forecast_date`` (inclusive).

    Parameters
    ----------
    df1, df2 : DataFrame
        Must have the same number of columns.
    first_forecast_date : str
        Quarter label, e.g. ``"2025Q4"``.
    dropna : bool, default False
        Drop any rows containing NA after concatenation.
    verbose : bool, default False
        Print helpful context.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
    """
    period = pd.Period(first_forecast_date, freq="Q")

    if df1.shape[1] != df2.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError("DataFrames must have the same number of columns.")

    df1_hist = df1.loc[: period - 1]
    df2_fcst = df2.loc[period:].copy()
    df2_fcst.columns = df1_hist.columns

    out = pd.concat([df1_hist, df2_fcst], axis=0)
    if dropna:
        out = out.dropna(how="any")
    if verbose:
        print("Joined at", period)
    return out


def annualize(df: pd.DataFrame, col: str, join_to_df: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame | pd.Series:
    """Compute annualized growth from a **level** column using pct_change.

    Formula: ``((1 + qoq) ** 4 - 1) * 100`` where ``qoq = df[col].pct_change()``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : DataFrame
    col : str
        Column that represents **levels**.
    join_to_df : bool, default True
        If True, add a new column ``f"{col}_ANN"`` and return the frame;
        else return the computed Series.
    """
    ann = ((1 + df[col].pct_change()) ** 4 - 1) * 100
    if join_to_df:
        df = df.copy()
        df[f"{col}_ANN"] = ann
        return df
    return ann


def join(df1: pd.DataFrame | pd.Series, df2: pd.DataFrame | pd.Series, *, bind: str, use_name: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Concatenate two objects either by rows (``bind='r'``) or columns (``bind='c'``).

    Parameters
    ----------
    df1, df2 : Series or DataFrame
    bind : {'r', 'c'}
        ``'r'`` → row-bind (stack); ``'c'`` → column-bind (side-by-side).
    use_name : {1, 2}, default 1
        For row-binding with mismatched column names, choose whose column names
        to keep: 1 → use ``df1`` names; 2 → use ``df2`` names.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
    """
    d1 = df1.to_frame() if isinstance(df1, pd.Series) else df1.copy()
    d2 = df2.to_frame() if isinstance(df2, pd.Series) else df2.copy()

    if bind == "r":
        if d1.shape[1] != d2.shape[1]:
            raise ValueError("Row-bind requires same number of columns.")
        if use_name == 1:
            d2.columns = d1.columns
        elif use_name == 2:
            d1.columns = d2.columns
        axis = 0
    elif bind == "c":
        axis = 1
    else:
        raise ValueError("bind must be 'r' or 'c'.")

    return pd.concat([d1, d2], axis=axis)


def yoy(
    df: pd.DataFrame | pd.Series,
    *,
    label: str = "_yoy",
    periods: int = 4,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Compute year-on-year % change using log-differences (×100).

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : Series or DataFrame of **levels**
    label : str, default "_yoy"
        Suffix to add to resulting column names (DataFrame case).
    periods : int, default 4
        Number of periods to lag for YoY (4 for quarterly data).
    verbose : bool, default False
        Print a preview.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        If input is a Series, returns a single-column DataFrame for consistency.
    """
    x = df.to_frame() if isinstance(df, pd.Series) else df
    temp = (np.log(x) - np.log(x).shift(periods)) * 100
    if label:
        temp.columns = [c if c.endswith(label) else f"{c}{label}" for c in temp.columns]
    if verbose:
        print(temp.dropna().tail())
    return temp


def to_q(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Ensure the index is a quarterly PeriodIndex.

    Returns a **copy** with ``freq='Q'`` PeriodIndex.
    """
    out = df.copy()
    out.index = pd.PeriodIndex(out.index, freq="Q")
    return out


def suffix(df: pd.DataFrame, label: str = "_yoy") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Append ``label`` to column names if not already present."""
    out = df.copy()
    out.columns = [c if c.endswith(label) else f"{c}{label}" for c in out.columns]
    return out


def conv_date(df: pd.DataFrame, period: str = "Q") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Convert a DatetimeIndex to a PeriodIndex.

    Currently supports quarterly (``period='Q'``).
    """
    if period.upper() != "Q":
        raise NotImplementedError("Only quarterly conversion is supported.")
    out = df.copy()
    out.index = pd.PeriodIndex(pd.to_datetime(out.index), freq="Q")
    return out


def repeat_last_row(df: pd.DataFrame, last_idx: str | pd.Period, n: int = 14) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Extend a frame by repeating the last row ``n`` more quarters.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : DataFrame
    last_idx : str or Period
        Label of the last historical quarter to anchor on.
    n : int, default 14
        Number of quarters to append by forward-filling the last row.
    """
    out = df.copy()
    last_idx = pd.Period(last_idx, freq="Q") if isinstance(last_idx, str) else last_idx
    start = out.index[0]
    extended_index = pd.period_range(start=start, periods=len(out) + n, freq="Q")
    out = out.reindex(extended_index)
    out.loc[last_idx:] = out.loc[last_idx:].ffill()
    return out


def demean(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Column-wise de-meaned copy of ``df``."""
    return df - df.mean()


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Growth/levels conversions
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def yoy_to_levels(
    yoy_rates_pct: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    first_forecast_date: str,
    levels_start: pd.DataFrame,
    annual: bool = True,
    lag: int = 4,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Convert YoY or QoQ growth paths into **levels** after a join point.

    Parameters
    ----------
    yoy_rates_pct : DataFrame
        Growth rates in percent units. If ``annual=True``, treat values as YoY
        growth; otherwise as QoQ growth.
    first_forecast_date : str
        The first quarter **to be computed** using the growth rates (e.g.,
        ``"2025Q4"``). ``levels_start`` must include the prior quarter level.
    levels_start : DataFrame
        Historical **levels** through at least the quarter **before**
        ``first_forecast_date`` for the same columns as ``yoy_rates_pct``.
    annual : bool, default True
        Interpret input rates as YoY if True; QoQ if False.
    lag : int, default 4
        Number of quarters in a year, used if ``annual=False``.
    verbose : bool, default False
        Print a tail preview.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        Levels series combining ``levels_start`` (up to join-1) and simulated
        levels thereafter.

    Notes
    -----
    - For annual YoY rates ``r_t`` (in percent), quarterly growth is
      ``g_t = (1 + r_t/100)**(1/4) - 1`` and ``L_t = L_{t-1} * (1 + g_t)``.
    - For QoQ rates ``q_t`` (percent), ``L_t = L_{t-1} * (1 + q_t/100)``.
    """
    period = pd.Period(first_forecast_date, freq="Q")

    # Align and prepare containers
    levels = levels_start.copy()
    rates = yoy_rates_pct.copy()

    # Ensure indexes are PeriodIndex(Q)
    levels.index = pd.PeriodIndex(levels.index, freq="Q")
    rates.index = pd.PeriodIndex(rates.index, freq="Q")

    # We will iteratively fill from period onward
    all_index = levels.index.union(rates.index)
    levels = levels.reindex(all_index)

    # Iterate only over the forecast path for clarity and stability
    cols = levels.columns.intersection(rates.columns)
    if cols.empty:
        raise ValueError("No overlapping columns between levels_start and yoy_rates_pct.")

    prev = period - 1
    if prev not in levels.index:
        raise KeyError(
            f"levels_start must include the quarter prior to {period} (i.e., {prev})."
        )

    for t in all_index[all_index.get_loc(period) :]:
        if t not in rates.index:
            # no new rate information; carry forward last level
            levels.loc[t, cols] = levels.loc[t - 1, cols]
            continue
        if annual:
            g = (1.0 + rates.loc[t, cols] / 100.0) ** (1.0 / 4.0) - 1.0
        else:
            g = rates.loc[t, cols] / 100.0
        levels.loc[t, cols] = levels.loc[t - 1, cols] * (1.0 + g)

    out = levels.loc[: all_index[-1], cols]
    if verbose:
        print(out.tail())
    return out


def annualize_qoq(qoq_pct: pd.Series | pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series | pd.DataFrame:
    """Convert QoQ percent changes into annualized percent changes.

    Formula: ``(1 + qoq/100)**4 - 1`` → ×100 percent units.
    """
    return ((1 + qoq_pct / 100.0) ** 4 - 1) * 100.0


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# File readers (MST packages, generic CSV/XLSX)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def read_mst_2025(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a specific 2025 MST Excel package format into a tidy quarterly frame.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path : str
        Path to the Excel file (sheet name "Fiscal Variable").

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        YoY percent changes with ``PeriodIndex(freq='Q')`` starting 2025Q4.
    """
    ex_ = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name="Fiscal Variable", header=None)
    ex = ex_.T
    ex.columns = ex.iloc[0]
    ex = ex.drop(ex.index[0]).reset_index(drop=True)
    mst_vars_yoy = ex.iloc[4:, 0:115]
    dates = pd.period_range("2025Q4", periods=len(mst_vars_yoy), freq="Q")
    mst_vars_yoy.index = dates
    return mst_vars_yoy


def plot_check(df1: pd.DataFrame, df2: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Quick-and-dirty plot to compare two frames side-by-side."""
    join(df1, df2, bind="c").plot()


def read(path: str, index_col: Optional[str] = None, sheet_name: Optional[str] = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read CSV or Excel and return a quarterly PeriodIndex-ed frame.

    Parameters
    ----------
    path : str
        File path. CSV is assumed when ``sheet_name`` is None.
    index_col : str, optional
        Column to use as index for CSV files. Defaults to ``"_date_"``.
    sheet_name : str, optional
        If provided, read the specified Excel sheet instead of CSV.
    """
    if sheet_name is None:
        idx = "_date_" if index_col is None else index_col
        df = pd.read_csv(path, index_col=idx)
        df.index = pd.to_datetime(df.index).to_period("Q")
        return df
    else:
        return pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet_name)


def read_mst(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read an MST CSV (OSFI stressed data) and return CA/US YoY percent changes.

    Expected CSV layout is transposed so that the useful variables are in rows
    after transformation.
    """
    df_mst = pd.read_csv(path).T
    df_mst.columns = ["a", "CA", "US", "b", "c"]
    df_mst = df_mst[["CA", "US"]].iloc[5:25]
    q_idx = pd.period_range(start="2025Q4", end="2030Q3", freq="Q")
    df_mst.index = q_idx
    mst_given_yoy = rmv_percent(df_mst, ["CA", "US"]).rename(
        columns={"CA": "CPICA_MST", "US": "CPIUS_MST"}
    )
    return mst_given_yoy


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Donor–target stress propagation (simple linear beta model)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ols_betas(y: np.ndarray, X: np.ndarray, *, add_intercept: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
    """Estimate OLS coefficients for ``y ~ X`` using least squares.

    Parameters
    ----------
    y : array-like, shape (T,)
    X : array-like, shape (T, K)
    add_intercept : bool, default False
        If True, include a column of ones in ``X``.
    """
    if y.ndim != 1:
        y = y.squeeze()
    if add_intercept:
        X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    return beta


def main(hist: pd.DataFrame, scen: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Estimate donor betas on history and apply them to scenario shocks.

    Targets: UK, AU, EA, JP; Donors: US, CA. All series are YoY percent changes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    hist : DataFrame
        Historical YoY percent-change data with columns:
        ``['CPIUS_TDBS','CPICA_TDBS','CPIUK_TDBS','CPIAU_TDBS','CPIEA_TDBS','CPIJP_TDBS']``
    scen : DataFrame
        Scenario window containing baseline (TDBS) and stressed (MST) YoY for US
        and CA, and baseline for targets.

    Returns
    -------
    DataFrame
        Stressed YoY for targets: ``CPIUK_MST, CPIAU_MST, CPIEA_MST, CPIJP_MST``
        with a quarterly PeriodIndex.
    """
    required_hist_cols = [
        "CPIUS_TDBS",
        "CPICA_TDBS",
        "CPIUK_TDBS",
        "CPIAU_TDBS",
        "CPIEA_TDBS",
        "CPIJP_TDBS",
    ]
    missing = [c for c in required_hist_cols if c not in hist.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"history is missing columns: {missing}")

    Z = demean(hist[required_hist_cols].dropna())
    donors = Z[["CPIUS_TDBS", "CPICA_TDBS"]].to_numpy()

    beta = {
        "UK": ols_betas(Z["CPIUK_TDBS"].to_numpy(), donors),
        "AU": ols_betas(Z["CPIAU_TDBS"].to_numpy(), donors),
        "EA": ols_betas(Z["CPIEA_TDBS"].to_numpy(), donors),
        "JP": ols_betas(Z["CPIJP_TDBS"].to_numpy(), donors),
    }

    required_scen_cols = [
        "CPICA_TDBS",
        "CPIUS_TDBS",
        "CPIUK_TDBS",
        "CPIAU_TDBS",
        "CPIEA_TDBS",
        "CPIJP_TDBS",
        "CPIUS_MST",
        "CPICA_MST",
    ]
    missing = [c for c in required_scen_cols if c not in scen.columns]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"scenario is missing columns: {missing}")

    scen = scen.copy()
    scen["US_SHOCK"] = scen["CPIUS_MST"] - scen["CPIUS_TDBS"]
    scen["CA_SHOCK"] = scen["CPICA_MST"] - scen["CPICA_TDBS"]

    shocks = scen[["US_SHOCK", "CA_SHOCK"]].to_numpy()

    scen["CPIUK_MST"] = scen["CPIUK_TDBS"].to_numpy() + shocks @ beta["UK"]
    scen["CPIAU_MST"] = scen["CPIAU_TDBS"].to_numpy() + shocks @ beta["AU"]
    scen["CPIEA_MST"] = scen["CPIEA_TDBS"].to_numpy() + shocks @ beta["EA"]
    scen["CPIJP_MST"] = scen["CPIJP_TDBS"].to_numpy() + shocks @ beta["JP"]

    out_cols = ["CPIUS_MST", "CPICA_MST", "CPIUK_MST", "CPIAU_MST", "CPIEA_MST", "CPIJP_MST"]
    smc_mst_yoy = scen[out_cols].copy()
    smc_mst_yoy.index = pd.PeriodIndex(smc_mst_yoy.index, freq="Q")

    print(
        "Estimated betas:\n"
        f" UK on US, CA: US={beta['UK'][0]:.3f}, CA={beta['UK'][1]:.3f}\n"
        f" AU on US, CA: US={beta['AU'][0]:.3f}, CA={beta['AU'][1]:.3f}\n"
        f" EA on US, CA: US={beta['EA'][0]:.3f}, CA={beta['EA'][1]:.3f}\n"
        f" JP on US, CA: US={beta['JP'][0]:.3f}, CA={beta['JP'][1]:.3f}"
    )
    return smc_mst_yoy


# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# End-to-end MST levels builder (example wiring)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mst_levels(
    pull_page: str,
    mst_forecast_yoy: pd.DataFrame,
    mst_vars: Sequence[str],
    jump_off: str,
    n: int = 13,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Construct MST **levels** series by combining actuals + stressed YoY.

    Steps (high-level)
    ------------------
    1. Pull baseline (TDBS) levels from EViews page ``pull_page``.
    2. Compute YoY for actuals and baseline forecast; splice in MST YoY from
       ``mst_forecast_yoy`` for the selected variables ``mst_vars``.
    3. Estimate donor betas on history and propagate US/CA shocks to targets.
    4. Extend to 2030Q3 + ``n`` quarters by repeating last row.
    5. Convert YoY to levels using :func:`yoy_to_levels` from ``jump_off``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pull_page : str
        EViews page name to pull.
    mst_forecast_yoy : DataFrame
        Stressed YoY in percent with columns like ``<VAR>_MST``.
    mst_vars : sequence of str
        Variable base names (e.g., ``["CPIAU","CPICA",...]``).
    jump_off : str
        Quarter where the MST forecast starts (e.g., ``"2025Q4"``).
    n : int, default 13
        Number of quarters to extend by repeating the last row.
    """
    jump_off_p = pd.Period(jump_off, freq="Q")

    # Build lists of baseline/stress names
    given_tdbs = [f"{v}_TDBS" for v in mst_vars]
    given_mst = [f"{v}_MST" for v in mst_vars]

    # 1) Pull baseline levels
    tdbs = get_page(pull_page)

    # 2) Compute YoY
    actuals = tdbs.loc[: jump_off_p - 1]
    tdbs_yoy = yoy(tdbs, label="")

    # Align actuals YoY to stress names and splice MST forecast
    actuals_yoy = yoy(actuals[given_tdbs], label="")
    actuals_yoy.columns = given_mst
    mst_actuals_yoy = join(actuals_yoy, mst_forecast_yoy[given_mst], bind="r")

    scenario_yoy = join(tdbs_yoy, mst_actuals_yoy, bind="c")
    hist = tdbs_yoy
    scen = scenario_yoy.loc[jump_off_p:].copy()

    # 3) Donor propagation
    smc_mst_yoy = main(hist, scen)

    # 4) Build levels container up to 2030Q3 and extend
    # Reorder/rename to match output columns from main
    tdbs_levels = tdbs.copy()
    tdbs_levels = tdbs_levels[["CPIAU", "CPICA", "CPIEA", "CPIJP", "CPIUK", "CPIUS"]]
    tdbs_levels.columns = ["CPIAU_MST", "CPICA_MST", "CPIEA_MST", "CPIJP_MST", "CPIUK_MST", "CPIUS_MST"]

    mixed_df = join(
        df1=tdbs_levels.loc[: "2025Q3"],
        df2=smc_mst_yoy.loc["2025Q4":],
        bind="r",
    )
    mixed_df_ext = repeat_last_row(mixed_df, "2030Q3", n=n)

    # 5) Convert YoY→levels post jump-off
    levels = yoy_to_levels(
        yoy_rates_pct=mixed_df_ext,
        first_forecast_date="2025Q4",
        levels_start=tdbs_levels,
        annual=True,
        verbose=False,
    )
    return levels
