docs.title: Python Setup Guide (TD Environment)
docs.text: This guide explains how to set up Python in the TD environment, install required packages, and run Jupyter notebooks.

docs.title: Step 1 – Request the TD Python Installer
docs.text:
Request the TD Python Installer for the Python Scripting Language from ServiceNow. There is no cost.

📎 Request Link

docs.title: Python Scripting Language
docs.text:
Python_PythonInstaller_1.0_ADM_R01

The TD Python Installer allows for selection of various supported versions of Python via a single package request. Installing the Python Installer package will add an Installer-Updater utility in your Windows Start Menu, which can be run to:

  • Select your version
  • Update your existing version

Using this package also configures setup to direct PyPI install requests through TD's Nexus Repository. This allows for installation of Python packages and libraries in a safe manner.

docs.title: Step 2 – Install Python
docs.text:
Once the Python Installer is in your Software Center, install the installer. Then, using the installer, install Python. For example, I installed Python 3.10, 64-bit.

Note

This is the base Python scripting language. Libraries are not packaged with the installer. This is a major difference from an Anaconda installation.

docs.title: Step 3 – Access the TD Nexus Repository
docs.text:
To install libraries, you need access to the TD Nexus Repository (repo.td.com). The repository provides a secure way (inside the TD firewall) to install Python libraries.

To obtain access, submit a ServiceNow request to join the TD_Engineer AD Group. There is no cost.

📎 Request Link

docs.title: AD Domain & Group Selection
docs.text:
• The AD Domain of the Group can be either BKNG.net or TDBFG.com.

!!! Note For Economics choose TDBFG.com

  • The AD Group TD_Engineer provides access to https://repo.td.com.

  • You can browse the available packages at: https://repo.td.com/repository/pypi-all/simple/

Important

Ensure you have Python installed from the Installer and confirm you can access https://repo.td.com before proceeding to the next steps.

docs.title: Step 4 – Export Your Current Python Libraries
docs.text:
Obtain a list of all Python libraries you currently have with Anaconda. This list will assist you when installing libraries in Python without Anaconda.

There is a text file with python libraries called requirements.txt, if you know the location of the requirements.txt you can use:

py -m pip install -rC:\Users\...\requirements.txt

This created a file named requirements.txt with a list of all installed libraries.

Note

You can get the txt file from a colleague.

docs.title: Step 5 – Create a Virtual Environment
docs.text:
1. Open a Windows Command Prompt:

  2. Enter cmd in the Windows Search bar.

  3. Verify that Python with PIP is installed by running: 

    py -m pip --version
    This will return the Python version and installation path.

  4. Create a virtual environment: 

    py -m venv path\\to\\location\\environment_name

Example: 

py -m venv C:\Users\tap9020\Python310\py_me
Here, the virtual environment is named py_me.

docs.title: Step 6 – Activate the Virtual Environment
docs.text:
To activate the environment, run: 

.\\environment_name\\Scripts\\activate

Example: 

.\\py_me\\Scripts\\activate

When activated, the command prompt will display the environment name (py_me).

Tip

If you get an error, try: 

C:\Users\...\Scripts\activate.bat

docs.title: Step 7 – Install Python Libraries
docs.text: The TD Repository (repo), within the TD firewall, provides access to packaged libraries. For example, installing pandas also installs numpy and other dependencies.

docs.title: Before installing libraries, ensure pip is updated:
docs.text: py -m pip install --upgrade pip

docs.title: Install libraries
docs.text:
Review your requirements.txt file and install required libraries. Example: 

py -m pip install pandas

If a specific version is required: 

py -m pip install pandas==1.1.3

Note

The repo may provide newer versions of some libraries. Be aware that syntax changes may occur if versions differ from your Anaconda environment.

docs.title: Step 8 – Install and Run Python with Jupyter Notebook
docs.text:
1. Open a Windows Command Prompt

  2. run 

    pip install jupyter

  3. Activate your virtual environment: 

    .\environment_name\Scripts\activate

  4. Navigate to your working directory: 
    cd \path\to\your\notebooks
  5. Launch Jupyter Notebook by typing into the following: 
    jupyter notebook

Jupyter will open, and notebooks originally created in Anaconda should run with minimal changes. In some cases, updated library versions may require small syntax adjustments.

Important

Make sure Jupyter is installed on your system (pip install jupyter)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Python provides the built-in re module for working with regular expressions.

import re

With this module you can: - Search text for patterns - Extract matches - Replace or remove matched substrings

docs.title: Substitution Example
docs.text:
Suppose you have the following code:

text = "C_coef * (dlog(hpius) - dlog(hpius_qef))"

You want to simplify it to:

C_coef * (dlog(hpius))

You can use:

import re

text = "C_coef * (dlog(hpius) - dlog(hpius_qef))"
new_text = re.sub(r"\s*-\s*dlog\(hpius_qef\)", "", text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)

The syntax for re.sub is:

re.sub(pattern, replacement_text, original_text, flags)

!!! note - \s* matches zero or more spaces - ( and ) escape literal parentheses - flags=re.IGNORECASE makes the match case-insensitive

docs.title: General Substitution Example
docs.text:
For a more general case:

import re

text = "C_coef * (dlog(hpius) - dlog(hpius_qef))"
new_text = re.sub(r"\s*-\s*dlog\([^(]+_qef\)", "", text)

This removes any substring of the form:

-dlog(x_qef)

regardless of the variable name inside.

docs.title: Python Regex Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
This section lists common regex patterns in Python, with both re.sub (replacement) and re.findall (extraction) examples. Always use raw strings r"..." to avoid escaping issues.

Note

  • [ ] → one character from this set

  • ( ) → a captured group, referenced as \1, \2, etc.

  • (?: ) → a non-capturing group (cannot be referenced)

docs.title: 1. Digits and Numbers
docs.text:
• One or more digits: \d+

    re.findall(r"\d+", "Order 123, item 45")   # ['123', '45']
re.sub(r"\d+", "#", "ID 123, item 45")     # 'ID #, item #'

  • Integer or decimal (with optional minus): -?\d+(?:\.\d+)? 

    re.findall(r"-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?", "3.14 -42 100")   # ['3.14', '-42', '100']

docs.title: 2. Words and Text
docs.text:
• Word characters: \w+

    `bash re.findall(r"\w+", "Hello, world!") # ['Hello', 'world']

  • Capitalized word: [A-Z][a-z]+

    re.findall(r"[A-Z][a-z]+", "Alice and Bob met Eve") # ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Eve']

Note

  • [A-Z][a-z]+ means: - one uppercase letter

  • followed by one or more lowercase letters

  • Specific alternatives (OR): cat|dog|bird

re.findall(r"cat|dog|bird", "a cat and a dog") # ['cat', 'dog']

docs.title: 3. Whitespace and Separators
docs.text:
• One or more whitespace: \s+

    re.split(r"\s+", "a   b\t c\n d")   # ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

  • Trim leading/trailing spaces: ^\s+|\s+$

    re.sub(r"^\s+|\s+$", "", "  padded  ")   # 'padded'

docs.title: 4. Anchors (Start/End)
docs.text:
• Start of string: ^pattern
  • End of string: pattern$
    re.match(r"^Hello", "Hello world") is not None   # True
re.sub(r"world$", "Earth", "Hello world")        # 'Hello Earth'

Note

  • ^pattern → match only at the very beginning
  • pattern$ → match only at the very end

docs.title: 5. Wildcards and Any Character
docs.text:
• Any char except newline: .

    re.findall(r"h.t", "hat hit hot hut")   # ['hat', 'hit', 'hot', 'hut']

  • Greedy anything: .*

  • Non-greedy anything: .*?
    re.findall(r"a.*b", "a---b a-b")      # ['a---b a-b']
re.findall(r"a.*?b", "a---b a-b")     # ['a---b', 'a-b']

Note

  • .* → greedy, matches as much as possible
  • .*? → non-greedy, matches as little as possible

docs.title: 6. Groups and Capturing
docs.text:
• Capture group: ( … )

    re.findall(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", "2025-08-21")
# [('2025', '08', '21')]

  • Backreference: (\w+) \1

    re.findall(r"(\w+) \1", "go go stop now now")   # ['go', 'now']

docs.title: 7. Repetitions
docs.text:
• Zero or more: a*
  • One or more: a+
  • Zero or one: a?
    re.findall(r"colou?r", "color colour")   # ['color', 'colour']

docs.title: 8. Lookarounds
docs.text:
• Positive lookahead: \d+(?=\sUSD)
  • Positive lookbehind: (?<=USD\s)\d+
    re.findall(r"\d+(?=\sUSD)", "100 USD, 200 EUR")   # ['100']
re.findall(r"(?<=USD\s)\d+", "USD 100 EUR 200")   # ['100']

Note

Lookaheads and lookbehinds assert context but do not consume characters.

docs.title: 9. Escaping Special Characters
docs.text:
• Literal dot: \.
  • Literal parentheses: \( and \)
    re.findall(r"\.", "a.b c")           # ['.']
re.findall(r"\(test\)", "(test)")    # ['(test)']

docs.title: 10. Practical Patterns
docs.text:
• Email: [\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+
  • URL: https?://\S+
  • Date (YYYY-MM-DD): \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}
  • Hex color: #[0-9A-Fa-f]{6}
    re.findall(r"https?://\S+", "Visit https://example.com")
# ['https://example.com']

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use re.sub for replacements and re.findall for extraction
  • Always use raw strings r"..."
  • Precompile patterns with re.compile() if reused often
